Prevention: Use certified or disease free seeds.
Maintain field sanitation: remove all debris and volunteer crops before transplanting.
If the disease is present in the soil practice crop rotation: break of three years and rotate with non host crops like maize, cabbage, beans or tomatoes.
Keep the area around onions weed free to increase air circulation, which will allow plants to dry rapidly from dew or irrigation water.
Consider control of onion thrips if they are present as they spread the disease.
Monitoring: Monitor onion plants from emergence once every week.
Initial symptoms are small white lesions mostly on the older leaves.
As the disease progresses the lesions enlarge and become purplish with light yellow concentric rings on the margins.
Leaves may turn yellowish-brown, lose erectness and eventually wilt, if the disease is not controlled.
Take action when first symptoms are seen.
Younger leaves become more susceptible as the bulb matures.
If the pathogen enters neck wounds during harvesting, bulbs can also be infected, making them to eventually become papery.
At harvest bulbs need to be checked for signs of the disease around the bulb neck.
Any affected bulbs should be destroyed as this disease can cause post-harvest losses.
Direct Control: Rogue out infected plants that show symptoms and burn.
